name: Mendeleev's Periodic Table
statement: Mendeleev arranged the elements so their properties repeated, and left gaps that predicted undiscovered ones.
statementAccent: left gaps that predicted undiscovered ones
meaning: Mendeleev's periodic table is the arrangement of the chemical elements devised by the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, first published in 1869, which organized the elements to reveal the periodic recurrence of their properties and became a foundation of modern chemistry. Mendeleev arranged the roughly sixty known elements in order of increasing atomic weight and grouped them so that elements with similar chemical properties fell into the same vertical columns. In doing so he discovered the periodic law: that the properties of the elements repeat periodically when they are ordered by weight. What made Mendeleev's table triumphant rather than merely tidy was his boldness in leaving gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered, and predicting the existence and detailed properties of several of them. He predicted, for instance, elements he called eka-aluminium, eka-boron, and eka-silicon, which were later found and named gallium, scandium, and germanium, with properties strikingly close to his predictions. He also corrected some accepted atomic weights to make elements fit their proper places. The accuracy of his predictions won wide acceptance for the periodic table, which, refined and reordered by atomic number in the twentieth century, remains one of the great unifying achievements of science.
mechanism: Mendeleev's table works by exploiting a regularity in the elements: when they are listed in order of increasing atomic weight, elements with similar chemical behaviour recur at regular intervals. Mendeleev laid the elements out in rows in order of weight and began new rows so that chemically similar elements, such as the reactive alkali metals or the inert-forming halogens, lined up in the same columns, called groups. This produced a grid in which position encodes chemistry: an element's group indicates its typical valence and reactivity, and its place in the sequence reflects its atomic weight. The crucial creative step was that Mendeleev trusted the pattern of properties over the raw ordering. Where placing an element strictly by weight would have put it in a chemically wrong column, he left a gap instead, reasoning that an undiscovered element belonged there, and he used the properties of the neighbouring elements above, below, and beside the gap to predict the missing element's atomic weight, density, and chemical behaviour. When gallium, scandium, and germanium were later discovered and matched his predictions closely, the gaps were filled and the periodic law vindicated. He similarly adjusted a few atomic weights that seemed to place elements wrongly. The deep reason the pattern exists, the structure of electron shells, was understood only later.

whyItMatters: Mendeleev's periodic table is one of the great unifying achievements in the history of science, organizing all the chemical elements into a single coherent system that reveals the deep order underlying their bewildering variety. By showing that the properties of the elements recur periodically, the periodic law gave chemistry a powerful organizing principle and a predictive framework, and the table became, and remains, the central icon and tool of the science. Its most celebrated triumph was predictive: because Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and forecast their properties, and because elements like gallium, scandium, and germanium were later found to match his forecasts, the table demonstrated that a good scientific theory can predict the unknown, one of the clearest historical examples of successful scientific prediction. The table guided the discovery and understanding of new elements, and its structure ultimately pointed toward the underlying physics of atomic structure and electron arrangement. Refined by ordering the elements by atomic number rather than weight, it continues to underpin all of chemistry, from teaching to research.

limits: Mendeleev's periodic table is foundational, but its priority and its basis both need qualification. The periodic system was not solely Mendeleev's discovery: John Newlands had proposed a related law of octaves in 1865, and Julius Lothar Meyer worked out a similar arrangement independently around the same time, so Mendeleev is credited chiefly because he published a full system, made bold and accurate predictions, and pressed the periodic law hardest, not because he alone conceived it. His ordering by atomic weight also produced a few anomalies, such as the pairing of tellurium and iodine, where the chemically correct order reverses the order of weights. These were resolved only in 1913, when Henry Moseley showed that the elements should be ordered by atomic number, the number of protons, rather than by weight, which is the basis of the modern table. The underlying reason for periodicity, electron shell structure, was unknown to Mendeleev.
misreadings: Mendeleev's periodic table was not his discovery alone; Newlands and Lothar Meyer had related systems, and Mendeleev is credited chiefly for his predictions and completeness. It is not ordered by atomic weight in its modern form, since Moseley showed in 1913 that atomic number gives the correct order, resolving anomalies like tellurium and iodine. And Mendeleev did not know why the properties repeat, the electron structure being discovered later, so treating the table as his sole invention, as fundamentally ordered by weight, or as resting on a known cause, misreads the periodic table's shared origin and later correction.
origin: The arrangement of the chemical elements published by the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, revealing the periodic law and predicting undiscovered elements; later reordered by atomic number after Moseley's work in 1913.
